b: I’m in a debate about the ethical implications of displaying artwork/imagery that evokes racism, sexism, anti-semitism, etc. when the original creator did not have that intent.

Two examples: 1) Bosch’s Garden of Earthly Delights. Scholars generally believe that the depictions of Africans in this and other pre-Enlightenment paintings were not intended to be racist. However, in the current post-colonial context, these depictions may evoke discomfort because of the similarity with racist caricatures that became popular after the painting. 2) Hindu/Jain/Buddhist ancient representations of the swastika. This was co-opted by the Nazis in the 1930s, but in South Asian cultures it still has positive symbolism. Nevertheless, many westerners may feel uncomfortable seeing a swastika because of the context in which they understand it. With that in mind, here’s the debate:

Other person’s argument: the intent of the artwork/imagery should govern whether it can be displayed. If the intent/cultural context of its creation was not discriminatory, the artwork can be displayed even if it means that someone may be uncomfortable observing it due to their interpretation that it’s discriminatory. It doesn’t matter who the person is who is displaying it. With this logic, Bosch’s Garden of Earthly Delights can be displayed in someone’s house even if a Black guest may be offended by the depiction. Likewise, it’s okay for anyone in the US to display an artwork containing an Indian swastika, despite a Jewish guest’s interpretation of it.

My position: even if the artwork/imagery was not created with discriminatory intent, the fact that it’s displayed in a current cultural context that’s likely to evoke discomfort, particularly for the marginalized group that the symbol has been used to harm, means it should not be displayed. So, Bosch’s Garden of Earthly Delights shouldn’t be displayed if a Black guest may be offended by the depiction, even though it wasn’t painted within a racist intent.

An exception I would carve out is that it the art/imagery could be displayed by the person whose culture still understands the symbol in its positive intent. So, an Indian Hindu in the US may still display artwork with the swastika — even though it may make a Jewish guest feel uncomfortable — but a white American should not because their cultural context of the swastika is an association with Nazi imagery.
(For the sake of this question, I’m putting aside the debate about whether having artwork/imagery from other cultures is appropriative.)
EDIT: Our specific debate is about displaying this kind of artwork/imagery in one’s own home knowing that a person of a marginalized identity that is implicated may be invited over as a guest.
